title: Entropy and Huffman codes
prompt:
Information theory. The symbols of a memoryless source occur with probabilities equal to their counts divided by the total count. Find the requested quantity in each of the following 12 independent situations:
1. a source emits the symbols A–G with relative frequencies proportional to A: 46, B: 17, C: 36, D: 41, E: 27, F: 52, G: 57 (out of 276); the Shannon entropy of the source in bits per symbol.
2. a source emits the symbols A–F with relative frequencies proportional to A: 53, B: 10, C: 5, D: 57, E: 50, F: 60 (out of 235); the average codeword length of an optimal binary Huffman code in bits per symbol.
3. a source emits the symbols A–F with relative frequencies proportional to A: 21, B: 59, C: 50, D: 17, E: 54, F: 3 (out of 204); the average codeword length of an optimal binary Huffman code in bits per symbol.
4. a source emits the symbols A–F with relative frequencies proportional to A: 47, B: 11, C: 57, D: 27, E: 27, F: 49 (out of 218); the redundancy of an optimal binary Huffman code (average codeword length minus entropy) in bits per symbol.
5. a source emits the symbols A–I with relative frequencies proportional to A: 28, B: 19, C: 27, D: 52, E: 44, F: 13, G: 30, H: 41, I: 40 (out of 294); the Shannon entropy of the source in bits per symbol.
6. a source emits the symbols A–G with relative frequencies proportional to A: 52, B: 28, C: 2, D: 49, E: 51, F: 55, G: 45 (out of 282); the redundancy of an optimal binary Huffman code (average codeword length minus entropy) in bits per symbol.
7. a source emits the symbols A–H with relative frequencies proportional to A: 48, B: 38, C: 49, D: 49, E: 34, F: 8, G: 22, H: 5 (out of 253); the average codeword length of an optimal binary Huffman code in bits per symbol.
8. a source emits the symbols A–E with relative frequencies proportional to A: 44, B: 8, C: 5, D: 52, E: 14 (out of 123); the redundancy of an optimal binary Huffman code (average codeword length minus entropy) in bits per symbol.
9. a source emits the symbols A–E with relative frequencies proportional to A: 35, B: 13, C: 14, D: 6, E: 27 (out of 95); the Shannon entropy of the source in bits per symbol.
10. a source emits the symbols A–G with relative frequencies proportional to A: 25, B: 12, C: 44, D: 7, E: 20, F: 43, G: 24 (out of 175); the Shannon entropy of the source in bits per symbol.
11. a source emits the symbols A–F with relative frequencies proportional to A: 4, B: 55, C: 17, D: 9, E: 23, F: 11 (out of 119); the redundancy of an optimal binary Huffman code (average codeword length minus entropy) in bits per symbol.
12. a source emits the symbols A–G with relative frequencies proportional to A: 17, B: 9, C: 15, D: 24, E: 7, F: 31, G: 42 (out of 145); the redundancy of an optimal binary Huffman code (average codeword length minus entropy) in bits per symbol.

Give the 12 requested values, each with 4 significant figures, in the order listed, as plain decimal numbers separated by commas.

Think it through, then finish with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <your answer>`.

title: M/M/c queues
prompt:
Queueing theory. Every system below is an M/M/c queue in steady state: Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, c identical servers, one first-come-first-served queue of unlimited length. Find the requested quantity in each of the following 13 independent systems:
1. customers arrive at 19.6 per hour and are served by a single server, each serving 26 customers per hour on average; average time in the system in minutes.
2. customers arrive at 22.1 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 16 customers per hour on average; probability that an arriving customer has to wait.
3. customers arrive at 3.2 per hour and are served by a single server, each serving 5 customers per hour on average; average waiting time in the queue in minutes.
4. customers arrive at 47.1 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 19 customers per hour on average; probability that an arriving customer has to wait.
5. customers arrive at 97.4 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 27 customers per hour on average; average number of customers waiting in the queue.
6. customers arrive at 14.0 per hour and are served by 3 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 12 customers per hour on average; average number of customers waiting in the queue.
7. customers arrive at 42.0 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 28 customers per hour on average; average time in the system in minutes.
8. customers arrive at 45.1 per hour and are served by 5 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 26 customers per hour on average; average waiting time in the queue in minutes.
9. customers arrive at 61.9 per hour and are served by 5 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 19 customers per hour on average; average number of customers waiting in the queue.
10. customers arrive at 78.3 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 27 customers per hour on average; average time in the system in minutes.
11. customers arrive at 18.7 per hour and are served by 4 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 6 customers per hour on average; probability that an arriving customer has to wait.
12. customers arrive at 57.3 per hour and are served by 3 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 26 customers per hour on average; probability that an arriving customer has to wait.
13. customers arrive at 16.3 per hour and are served by 5 identical servers sharing one queue, each serving 6 customers per hour on average; probability that an arriving customer has to wait.

Give the 13 requested values, each with 4 significant figures, in the order listed, as plain decimal numbers separated by commas.

Think it through, then finish with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <your answer>`.

title: Great-circle distance and initial course
prompt:
Navigation on a spherical Earth of radius 6371 km. For each of the following 7 pairs of points find the requested quantity of the shortest (great-circle) route:
1. from 66.6° S, 151.6° E to 48.0° N, 177.4° E; great-circle distance in km.
2. from 50.0° S, 71.6° E to 17.0° N, 61.7° E; initial true bearing (course) of the great-circle route from the first point, in degrees from 0 to 360.
3. from 15.7° N, 125.3° W to 17.2° N, 92.3° E; initial true bearing (course) of the great-circle route from the first point, in degrees from 0 to 360.
4. from 57.9° S, 77.9° E to 47.3° S, 114.7° E; great-circle distance in km.
5. from 36.4° N, 54.7° E to 1.2° N, 131.7° W; great-circle distance in km.
6. from 9.9° N, 104.3° W to 19.1° N, 143.2° W; initial true bearing (course) of the great-circle route from the first point, in degrees from 0 to 360.
7. from 64.0° S, 33.2° E to 12.2° N, 141.2° W; initial true bearing (course) of the great-circle route from the first point, in degrees from 0 to 360.

Give the 7 requested values, each with 4 significant figures, in the order listed, as plain decimal numbers separated by commas.

Think it through, then finish with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <your answer>`.

title: Composition of rotations in R³
prompt:
Rotations of R³ about the coordinate axes; a positive angle is counter-clockwise when looking from the positive end of the axis towards the origin (right-hand rule). The following 7 rotations are applied in this order, each to the result of the previous ones (all about the fixed coordinate axes):
1. rotation by -149° about the y-axis
2. rotation by 127° about the x-axis
3. rotation by -30° about the x-axis
4. rotation by -47° about the z-axis
5. rotation by 9° about the x-axis
6. rotation by -18° about the z-axis
7. rotation by 15° about the y-axis

Let R be the resulting rotation. Find the image R·v of v = (-9, -5, 7) and the rotation angle of R (between 0° and 180°). Give 4 values — the three coordinates of R·v and the angle in degrees — each with 4 significant figures, as plain decimal numbers separated by commas.

Think it through, then finish with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <your answer>`.

title: Determinant of an integer matrix
prompt:
Compute the determinant of the following 7×7 integer matrix A.

A =
[ -4   1   3   1  -3   1  -3 ]
[  4   2   0  -1  -3   2   0 ]
[ -2   0  -1   2   2  -3   2 ]
[ -2  -4   3   3  -1   2   2 ]
[ -3   4  -3  -1  -4  -2   1 ]
[ -1  -4   2  -1  -3   3  -4 ]
[  0   2  -1   2   2   0   2 ]

Give the exact value as an integer.

Think it through, then finish with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <your answer>`.
